answer.body_markdown:
Here are the key Medicare changes for GLP‑1 coverage in 2026:

**The Medicare GLP‑1 Bridge Program (July 1, 2026 – Dec. 31, 2027)**
- For the first time, Medicare is providing a temporary but direct pathway to cover GLP‑1 medications **prescribed for weight loss** (obesity). Historically such use was excluded from Part D.
- Eligible Part D enrollees can get covered drugs for a **flat $50/month copay**.
- Covered medications include:
  - **Foundayo** (orforglipron oral tablet)
  - **Wegovy** (semaglutide) – pills and injections
  - **Zepbound** (tirzepatide) **KwikPens only** (single-use pens and vials are excluded)
- Note: **Ozempic** and **Mounjaro** remain covered only for their diabetes indication under standard Part D, and are **not** included in this Bridge program for weight loss.

**The BALANCE Model delayed**
- CMS had announced the voluntary **BALANCE** program in late 2025 as a longer-term solution for Medicare and Medicaid to negotiate lower prices and expand GLP‑1 access.
- Due to insurer concerns, Medicare **delayed the Part D portion** of BALANCE; the **Bridge program** is serving as the interim solution. The Medicaid portion of BALANCE is still moving forward.

**General Part D cost protection in 2026**
- All Part D enrollees also benefit from a new **$2,000 annual cap on out-of-pocket prescription costs**, which helps limit total spending if a GLP‑1 is covered under any approved indication.

answer.body_markdown:
**Yes, a nurse practitioner can order a continuous glucose monitor (CGM) under Medicare** if they meet the definition of a "treating practitioner" and practice requirements.

## Authority to Order
Under Medicare DMEPOS rules, a **"treating practitioner"** is defined as:
- A physician; **or**
- A physician assistant, **nurse practitioner**, or clinical nurse specialist (as defined in Social Security Act §1861(aa)(5)) [^1^][^2^]

A nurse practitioner may sign the order if they:
- Are treating the beneficiary for the condition requiring the CGM
- Are practicing independently of a physician
- Bill Medicare for other covered services using their own provider number
- Are permitted to do so under their state’s scope of practice laws [^3^]

## What the Order Must Contain
The order must be a **Standard Written Order (SWO)** with all of the following elements [^1^][^4^][^5^]:

| Required Element | Details |
|---|---|
| **Beneficiary name or MBI** | Medicare Beneficiary Identifier |
| **Description of item** | General description, brand/model, HCPCS code, or narrative |
| **Quantity** | To be dispensed (if applicable) |
| **Order date** | Date the order is written |
| **Treating practitioner name or NPI** | National Provider Identifier |
| **Treating practitioner signature** | Must meet CMS signature requirements |

## Additional CGM-Specific Requirements
Before ordering, the treating practitioner must also:
- Conduct an **in-person or Medicare-approved telehealth visit within 6 months** prior to ordering to evaluate diabetes control and confirm eligibility [^6^][^7^]
- Confirm the patient meets coverage criteria (e.g., insulin-treated or history of problematic hypoglycemia as defined by CMS)
- Document that the CGM is prescribed to improve glycemic control

For continued coverage, the treating practitioner must assess the patient **every 6 months** to document adherence to the CGM regimen and diabetes treatment plan [^6^][^7^].

- [^3^] CMS, Medicare Program Integrity Manual — Nurse Practitioner Order Rules (PDF): https://www.cms.gov/Regulations-and-Guidance/Guidance/Transmittals/Downloads/R618PI.pdf
- [^4^] CMS, Standard Documentation Requirements for All Claims (A55426): https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/article.aspx?articleid=55426

answer.body_markdown:
For Medicare to cover a Continuous Glucose Monitor (CGM), the following practitioner visit requirements must be met:

## Initial Coverage Visit
As part of the **initial provision** of a CGM, the treating practitioner must conduct an **in-person or Medicare-approved telehealth visit** with the beneficiary. The medical record from that visit must document that:
1. The beneficiary has **diabetes mellitus**
2. The beneficiary (or caregiver) has received **appropriate training** in the use of the CGM, evidenced by a prescription
3. The CGM is prescribed in accordance with **FDA indications for use**
4. The CGM is prescribed to improve glycemic control for a beneficiary who is **insulin-treated** or has a **history of problematic hypoglycemia**

## Continued Coverage Visit
To justify **continued coverage**, the treating practitioner must conduct an **in-person or Medicare-approved telehealth visit with the beneficiary every 6 months** following the initial prescription. The visit must document:
- The beneficiary's **adherence to their CGM regimen and diabetes treatment plan**
- That the supplies remain **medically necessary**

**Note:** There is no requirement for the practitioner to reconfirm that the initial coverage criteria are met for continued coverage—only the 6-month adherence visit is required.

Failure to document this 6-month visit can result in insufficient documentation errors and payment recoupment.

- **Benefit category:** Covered as **durable medical equipment (DME)** under Part B.
- **Eligibility:** Expanded in 2023/2025 to include people with diabetes on basal insulin OR those who have documented problematic low blood glucose events. The prescribing practitioner must see the patient every 6 months.
- **Cost sharing:** After you meet the annual **Part B deductible ($257 in 2025)**, you pay **20% coinsurance** of the Medicare-approved amount—provided your doctor and DME supplier are enrolled in Medicare and accept assignment.
- **Supplemental coverage:** If you have a Medigap plan, it may cover that 20% coinsurance, reducing your out-of-pocket cost significantly.

Sources: [Medicare.gov – CGM Coverage](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/continuous-glucose-monitors), [AARP – Medicare CGM Coverage](https://www.aarp.org/medicare/does-medicare-cover-continuous-glucose-monitors)

---

## GLP-1 Medications: **Medicare Part D**
- **Benefit category:** Covered under Medicare Part D (prescription drug plans), but **only when prescribed for certain FDA-approved conditions other than weight loss alone** due to a statutory exclusion. Covered indications include:
  - **Type 2 diabetes** (e.g., Ozempic, Mounjaro, Rybelsus)
  - **Cardiovascular risk reduction** (e.g., Wegovy for adults with heart disease + obesity/overweight)
  - **Obstructive sleep apnea** (e.g., Zepbound)
- **Cost sharing:** GLP-1s are often placed on **high/specialty tiers**. Plans commonly require **coinsurance of roughly 25–33%** of the drug’s price. Depending on the drug and plan, this can mean roughly **$325–$430+ per month** out of pocket before hitting the annual cap.
- **2025 Part D cap:** Thanks to the Inflation Reduction Act, total **Part D out-of-pocket spending is capped at $2,000 per year** (2025 onward). This cap does **not** apply to drugs covered under Part B.
- **Prior authorization:** Near-universal in 2025 for GLP-1s. Your doctor must document the covered diagnosis (e.g., diabetes, cardiovascular disease).

Sources: [U.S. News – Medicare GLP-1 Coverage](https://health.usnews.com/medicare/articles/does-medicare-cover-ozempic), [KFF – BALANCE Model for GLP-1s](https://www.kff.org/medicare/what-to-know-about-the-balance-model-for-glp-1s-in-medicare-and-medicaid), [JAMA Network – Part D Costs for GLP-1s](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12461600)

---

### What About Weight Loss?
Federal law still bars standard Part D coverage for weight loss alone. However:
- Starting **July 1, 2026**, the temporary **Medicare GLP-1 Bridge program** will allow eligible Part D enrollees to obtain certain weight-loss GLP-1s (Wegovy, Foundayo, Zepbound KwikPen) for a **$50 monthly copay**.
- Important: That **$50 copay does NOT count** toward your Part D deductible or the $2,000 annual out-of-pocket maximum.

Source: [Medicare.gov – Weight Loss Drugs](https://www.medicare.gov/coverage/weight-loss-drugs)

---

### Bottom Line on Cost Impact
| Feature | CGM (Part B) | GLP-1 (Part D) |
|---|---|---|
| **Typical cost sharing** | 20% coinsurance after deductible | Coinsurance (often 25–33%) or high copays |
| **Annual out-of-pocket cap?** | No cap under Part B | Capped at **$2,000/year** (2025+) |
| **Medigap help?** | Often yes (covers 20%) | No standard Medigap coverage for Part D |
| **Prior authorization** | Minimal; documentation required | Very common (99%+ in 2025) |

In short, CGM coverage under Part B tends to be more predictable and modest in cost sharing, especially if you have Medigap, while GLP-1 coverage under Part D can involve high monthly costs until you hit the $2,000 annual limit.

answer.body_markdown:
The CMS Innovation Center model is called the **BALANCE Model** (Better Approaches to Lifestyle and Nutrition for Comprehensive hEalth). It is a voluntary program in which CMS negotiates lower net prices and standardized coverage terms with GLP-1 manufacturers for weight-management and metabolic health drugs.

**Start Dates:**

- **Medicaid:** The BALANCE Model is scheduled to launch in **May 2026** for state Medicaid agencies that choose to participate.  
- **Medicare Part D:** The BALANCE Model has been **indefinitely delayed** from its original January 2027 start date due to insurer concerns. In its place, CMS is running the **Medicare GLP-1 Bridge** demonstration from **July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2027**, which provides eligible Part D beneficiaries access to certain GLP-1s outside of the standard Part D benefit while CMS collects additional utilization data.

**Sources:**
- CMS Innovation Center: BALANCE Model overview and participant information ([cms.gov](https://www.cms.gov/priorities/innovation/innovation-models/balance))
- KFF analysis of the BALANCE Model and Medicare GLP-1 Bridge timeline ([kff.org](https://www.kff.org/medicare/what-to-know-about-the-balance-model-for-glp-1s-in-medicare-and-medicaid))
- Fierce Healthcare reporting on the Part D delay and bridge extension ([fiercehealthcare.com](https://www.fiercehealthcare.com/payers/cms-delays-part-d-glp-1-model-amid-skepticism-insurers))

answer.body_markdown:
**Short answer:** it depends entirely on the payer, but under **traditional Medicare criteria, generally no** for a patient with type 2 diabetes who is on metformin alone and does **not** have documented problematic hypoglycemia.

Here is how major payers typically handle this:

| Payer / Program | CGM for metformin-only T2D? | Typical criteria |
|---|---|---|
| **Medicare (CMS)** | **Not covered** unless problematic hypoglycemia is documented | Must be **insulin-treated** **OR** have documented recurrent level 2 hypoglycemia (<54 mg/dL) despite med adjustments, or one level 3 event requiring assistance. The KX modifier must **not** be used for beneficiaries exclusively on oral agents like metformin. |
| **Commercial plans** | **Sometimes**, but often requires prior authorization | Policies vary widely. Some plans still require insulin therapy; others have begun covering non–insulin-treated T2D if glycemic targets are not being met or based on plan-specific InterQual/medical necessity criteria. |
| **Medicaid** | **Varies by state** | Many states limit CGM to insulin-treated individuals or type 1 diabetes. Some are broadening access, but criteria differ significantly. |

### Key details from current policies:
- **Medicare** explicitly states that beneficiaries treated **exclusively with oral hypoglycemic agents** do not meet standard therapeutic CGM coverage requirements unless they have a documented history of problematic hypoglycemia (recurrent level 2 events or a single level 3 event) ([CMS Policy Article A52464](https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/article.aspx?articleId=52464), [Dexcom Medicare FAQ](https://www.dexcom.com/en-us/faqs/medicare), [Doko MD summary](https://doko.md/medicare-cover-cgm-type-2-diabetes)).
- **UnitedHealthcare** references 2024 evidence showing CGM improves glycemic control in non–insulin-treated type 2 diabetes, but coverage still depends on meeting plan-specific medical necessity criteria, often through prior authorization ([UnitedHealthcare policy PDF](https://www.uhcprovider.com/content/dam/provider/docs/public/policies/comm-medical-drug/continuous-glucose-monitoring-insulin-delivery-managing-diabetes.pdf)).
- **Over-the-counter CGMs** (e.g., Abbott Libre Rio) are now marketed specifically for adults with type 2 diabetes not using insulin, but these are typically patient-pay retail products and may not be covered by insurance as DME/pharmacy benefits ([BCBSRI policy](https://www.bcbsri.com/providers/medicalpolicies/files/glucose-monitoring-continuous)).

### Bottom line for your patient:
If this is a **Medicare** patient on metformin alone without qualifying hypoglycemia, you likely **cannot approve** a CGM under current Medicare coverage rules.  
If this is a **commercially insured** patient, you should check the specific plan’s prior authorization policy—coverage for non-insulin T2D is expanding but is not universal.

**Source URLs:**
- https://www.cms.gov/medicare-coverage-database/view/article.aspx?articleId=52464
- https://www.dexcom.com/en-us/faqs/medicare
- https://doko.md/medicare-cover-cgm-type-2-diabetes
- https://www.uhcprovider.com/content/dam/provider/docs/public/policies/comm-medical-drug/continuous-glucose-monitoring-insulin-delivery-managing-diabetes.pdf
- https://www.bcbsri.com/providers/medicalpolicies/files/glucose-monitoring-continuous
